drills.q: What are the three parts of an Azure RBAC role assignment, and how does that differ structurally from an AWS IAM policy?
drills.a: Security principal, role definition, and scope. AWS bundles actions and resource ARNs together in one policy document attached to an identity; Azure decouples the permission set (role definition) from the resource target (scope), letting the same role definition be reused at many different scopes.

drills.q: Explain Azure RBAC scope inheritance and name the four levels of the hierarchy.
drills.a: Management group -> subscription -> resource group -> resource. A role assigned at a higher level is automatically inherited by everything beneath it -- an actual cascading grant, unlike anything in AWS IAM.

drills.q: A user with Contributor at subscription scope asks you to also let them grant a teammate access. What's wrong with just giving them more Contributor-adjacent permissions, and what's the correct fix?
drills.a: Contributor structurally excludes roleAssignments/write regardless of scope -- it can never grant access to others, no matter how broadly it's assigned. The correct fix is assigning User Access Administrator (scoped as narrowly as possible) or Owner, not a bigger Contributor grant.

drills.q: What does Azure have as the closest analog to an AWS SCP, and why is it a weaker guarantee?
drills.a: Deny assignments (usually auto-generated by Blueprints/Landing Zones or Lighthouse delegation, rarely hand-authored) plus Azure Policy's deny effect. Policy governs resource configuration state, not identity permission ceilings -- it can't express 'this principal may never call this API' the way an SCP denies an action outright; RBAC itself is purely additive with no ceiling concept at all.

drills.q: Compare the lifecycle of system-assigned vs user-assigned managed identities and explain why one is safer for a VM Scale Set.
drills.a: System-assigned identities are created 1:1 with a resource and die when it's deleted; user-assigned identities are independent resources with their own lifecycle, attachable to up to 1,000 resources. A scale set with system-assigned identities loses role assignments on every instance replacement; user-assigned identities survive instance churn since they're attached to the scale set model, not tied to individual instance lifecycles.

drills.q: Walk through the mechanics of a managed identity token request, including the anti-SSRF hardening.
drills.a: The workload calls the local IMDS endpoint (169.254.169.254/metadata/identity/oauth2/token) with a required 'Metadata: true' header and target audience URI; IMDS returns a short-lived Entra ID token. The header requirement raises the bar against naive SSRF-via-open-redirect attacks that can't set custom headers, mirroring AWS's IMDSv2 token hardening.

drills.q: What Conditional Access and PIM capabilities does a free-tier Entra ID tenant lack, and why does that matter compared to AWS?
drills.a: Zero Conditional Access at all (requires P1 minimum) -- no MFA enforcement policy, no device-compliance gating; and no risk-based sign-in blocking or PIM even with P1, since those require P2. AWS provides baseline MFA options and identity risk signals (IAM, GuardDuty) without a separate paid identity tier, so 'we can't afford identity security yet' is a materially riskier statement on Azure's free tier.

drills.q: Explain what Continuous Access Evaluation (CAE) does and give a concrete scenario where its absence matters.
drills.a: CAE revokes tokens within minutes of a critical signal (account disabled, password changed, high risk) instead of waiting for natural 60-90 minute token expiry. Scenario: an employee's laptop is stolen with an active session; without CAE, the stolen token stays valid up to 90 minutes after IT disables the account, whereas CAE-enabled services cut it off almost immediately -- but only for services that explicitly implement CAE support.

drills.q: A subscription's deployment automation starts failing with role-assignment errors, but the team doesn't believe they're near any quota. What do you check, and what's the fix?
drills.a: Check total role assignments against the hard 4,000-per-subscription ceiling, which accumulates silently across every resource group/resource scope over years and isn't raisable. Fix: consolidate individual-principal assignments into group-based assignments (one group assignment covers all members) and audit for stale assignments from decommissioned environments; PIM-eligible and future-scheduled assignments don't count against the limit.

drills.q: Design least-privilege RBAC and identity for a CI/CD pipeline deploying across dev/staging/prod subscriptions, and explain why subscription-wide Contributor is the wrong shortcut.
drills.a: Use a user-assigned managed identity or Workload ID Federation (OIDC, no stored secret) with Contributor scoped per-environment resource group, never subscription-wide or Owner; gate prod with human-approval pipeline steps and PIM-eligible break-glass roles for operators. Subscription-wide Contributor means a single compromised pipeline identity can touch every environment including prod from one foothold, violating blast-radius containment.

drills.q: State the exact numeric limits for managed identity attachment and creation rate.
drills.a: A user-assigned identity attaches to up to 1,000 resources; a single resource can have up to 20 user-assigned identities. Creation is rate-limited to 400 ops/20s per tenant/region and 80 ops/20s per subscription/region.
